title: Fewest Distinct Values After Removals
statement:
You get an array nums and a number k. Remove exactly k elements (any positions you like).

Return the smallest possible number of distinct values left in the array.

examples.why: Removing both 9s wipes out one value. The third removal cannot finish off 4 or 2, which appear 3 times each.
Spend the removals on the rare values 6 and 8. Removing two 5s would leave all three values.
Everything is removed, so no values are left.

hints: Positions do not matter. Only how many times each value appears.
A value disappears only when all of its copies are removed. Which values are cheapest to wipe out?
Sort the counts from smallest to largest and spend k on them in that order until the next one does not fit.

explain.intuition:
Removing a value costs exactly its count. Removing part of a value's copies changes nothing about the distinct count. So the question is: how many whole values can you pay for with a budget of k?

To fit the most items into a budget, buy the cheapest first. Any plan that wipes out some value with a larger count could swap it for a cheaper one and do at least as well. Leftover removals after the last full value are simply spent on partial copies, which is always possible.
steps: Count how many times each value appears.
Sort the counts in increasing order.
Walk through them: while k ≥ count, subtract it from k and mark that value as gone.
Stop at the first count that does not fit. Return the number of values that were not marked gone.
pitfalls: Removing the most frequent value first. That is the opposite of what helps.
Using k > count instead of k ≥ count: a value that exactly uses up the remaining budget still disappears.
Continuing after a count does not fit. Sorted counts only grow, so no later value fits either.

complexity.time: O(n log n), or O(n) with counting buckets

solutions.title: Try every set of values to remove
solutions.idea: For each subset of distinct values, check whether their total count is at most k. Keep the largest such subset.
solutions.time: O(2ᵈ · d) for d distinct values

solutions.title: Sort counts, remove the cheapest values first
solutions.idea: Wiping out a value costs its count. Spend k on the smallest counts.

solutions.title: Bucket the counts
solutions.idea: Counts are at most n, so group values by count in an array instead of sorting, then spend k from the smallest count up.

followups: Return which values remain, not just how many.
Now k is the number of values you may remove entirely, and you want to keep as many elements as possible. What changes?
